title: 禪宗頌古聯珠通集 (Anthology of Chan Verse Commentaries on Koans, 40 juan)
shelf_note: Faying's Song compilation with Puhui's Yuan continuation, a core gongan-verse anthology. Pages show the Wanli-period 支那撰述 canon blocks. Squarely Chan.
structure_note: Each image is an open spread (the b-face of one leaf and the a-face of the next), so every record covers two half-leaves. printed_backsteps 67 and repeats 165 against only 204 pages with a printed number fit spreads that carry two folio numbers, plus juan restarts (p836 ends juan 35 and starts juan 36). This looks like how the scan is cut, not a broken order. OCR on 952 of 956 pages. The translated count disagrees (950 counted vs pages_translated field 938): a stale counter.

reader_summary: This is the Song–Yuan anthology of verse comments on Chan gongan, scanned at the Library of Congress from a Wanli-era printing, with two half-leaves per image. The transcription follows the right text closely line by line, but it misses editorial markers and a whole colophon, and it sometimes slips a character that changes the sense. The English reads well and follows the verse. Names and a few lines need checking against the image.
book_verdict: A sound and important witness with mostly accurate transcription. On-sight problems are the dropped 1597 colophon, an invented header and folio number, and a few meaning-changing misreads carried into the English.

title: 石門文字禪·卷二十九~卷三十 (vol 11)
shelf_note: Juemin Huihong's (德洪) collected writings, from the Siku Quanshu manuscript (欽定四庫全書 in the margins). This is Chan literary prose: letters, stupa inscriptions and sacrificial texts. The catalogue's only collection, 'universallibrary', is an IA bucket, not a curated shelf.
structure_note: This is one fascicle (juan 29–30) of a multi-volume set. The printed folio number restarts at each juan, which explains the backsteps and repeats. 120 of 122 pages are translated. The OCR puts the juan label (卷二十九, 卷三十) into <page-num>.

reader_summary: This is part of Huihong's 'Chan of Words and Letters' in the clean Siku Quanshu manuscript copy, with letters, a stupa record of Zhenjing Kewen, and memorial texts. On a clean page the transcription is close to exact. One page skips a whole column, and the English then gives Guishan's words to the narrator. Where the column count is intact the English is accurate and readable.
book_verdict: A clean witness with good translation on most pages. One dropped column (p45) produces a misattributed speech that a specialist would catch at once.

title: Jikji (직지심체요절, Anthology of Great Buddhist Priests' Zen Teachings)
shelf_note: Baegun's 1377 Korean Seon anthology, the BnF copy of the surviving second volume (the margin reads 直指下). It is Chan/Seon encounter dialogue throughout.
structure_note: 86 records, including binding and edge photographs (p86 is a spine/edge view, not a text leaf). A few printed backsteps (3) fit leaf numerals with the cover and edge shots mixed in. 82 of 86 are translated. Nothing looks broken.

reader_summary: This is the BnF copy of the Jikji, volume two, printed with metal type in 1377: a Korean Seon selection of patriarchs' sayings. The transcription is of the right text but slips on the uneven metal type, including a dropped line in Dongshan's best-known verse and a misread personal name. The English follows the dialogues fluently, but where the OCR slipped it either carries the error or quietly restores the line from memory.
book_verdict: A famous and correct witness on the right shelf. Line-level OCR losses on uneven metal type (p28 verse, p20 name) mean a scholar should read it with the image open.

title: 六祖大師法寶壇經 (Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch)
shelf_note: The Zongbao (Yuan) recension of the Platform Sutra, a central Chan text.
structure_note: 44 pages, all with OCR and translation. The single printed number fits an unpaginated digital typescript. Nothing is broken, but the 'scan' is a modern e-text rendered as images.

ocr_errors.image: 不念利益成壞等事 / 正法眼藏傳付何人

tr_errors.english: <note>…a historical attempt to steal the Sixth Patriarch's head by a monk hired by a rival school…</note>
tr_errors.problem: invented detail. In the traditional account Zhang Jingman was hired by the Korean monk Kim Taebi, not by a rival school

reader_summary: This is the standard Zongbao text of the Platform Sutra. The images are a modern typeset e-text, not a historical print, so the transcription is almost exact. The English is careful and trustworthy, apart from one invented note. A scholar will ask what edition this is and where the typescript came from, and the page does not say.
book_verdict: Accurate transcription and good translation. But the source is a modern digital typescript with no stated origin, which makes it a rights and provenance question rather than a historical witness.
